concepts.title: Unit Testing with describe/it/expect
concepts.description: A test framework like Jest gives structure (describe/it) and a fluent assertion library (expect) to what would otherwise be ad-hoc scripts full of console.log and manual comparisons -- understanding how a test actually fails, and why isolated, repeatable unit tests matter, is the foundation everything else in testing builds on.
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose of describe and it (or test) blocks and how they organize related assertions into readable, isolated units.
Write assertions with expect using matchers like toBe, toEqual, toThrow, and toHaveLength, and explain when toBe is wrong and toEqual is required.
Explain what makes a test 'unit' rather than 'integration' -- isolating the function under test from its collaborators.
Use beforeEach/afterEach to reset shared state between tests and explain why leaking state across tests produces order-dependent failures.
Predict whether a given assertion passes or fails, and explain the specific mismatch a failing assertion reports.

sections.heading: Why Not Just console.log Everything?
describe and it: Organizing Related Assertions
expect and Matchers: toBe vs toEqual, and the Rest
sections.body:
expect(value) returns an object with chainable matcher methods that describe what you expect to be true about value. The two most common, and the two people mix up most often, are toBe and toEqual. **toBe** uses Object.is-style strict equality -- effectively === -- which is exactly right for primitives (numbers, strings, booleans) but wrong for objects and arrays, because two different array instances with identical contents are never === to each other. **toEqual** instead performs a recursive, structural (deep) comparison -- it checks that every key and value inside an object or array matches, regardless of whether the two are literally the same object in memory.

```javascript
expect(2 + 2).toBe(4);                       // correct: primitives compare by value with toBe
expect({ id: 1 }).toEqual({ id: 1 });         // correct: toEqual compares structure
expect({ id: 1 }).toBe({ id: 1});             // FAILS -- two different object instances, never === 
```

Other matchers worth knowing from the start: toThrow(message) asserts a function call throws (note: you must pass a function, expect(() => risky()).toThrow(), not expect(risky()).toThrow() -- the latter calls risky() immediately, outside Jest's control, before expect ever gets a chance to catch anything). toHaveLength(n) checks an array's or string's .length. toContain(item) checks array membership or substring presence. toBeNull, toBeUndefined, and toBeDefined check for those specific values precisely, which matters because == comparisons would treat null and undefined as interchangeable in ways a strict test shouldn't. Prefixing any matcher with .not (expect(x).not.toBe(y)) inverts it. Picking the matcher that actually matches your intent -- structural vs reference equality being the single most common mistake -- is what makes a test either genuinely useful or a false sense of security.

examples.title: A Small Module and Its Full Test Suite
examples.explanation: Each it block tests exactly one behavior of slugify, phrased as a sentence describing what should be true -- this is deliberate: when 'collapses multiple internal spaces into one hyphen' fails, the test name alone tells you which specific behavior regressed, without needing to read the assertion itself first. All three tests call toBe rather than toEqual because slugify returns a primitive string, where reference equality and value equality are the same thing -- toEqual would also have worked here, but toBe is the more precise signal to a reader that a primitive comparison is intended.

examples.title: toBe vs toEqual in Practice
examples.explanation: The commented-out toBe line would fail every single time, no matter how correct createUser's logic is, because user and the literal object passed to toBe are two distinct objects in memory -- === is false for any two separately-created objects even with identical contents. toEqual walks both objects recursively, comparing keys and values (including nested arrays, like roles), and considers them equal based on structure rather than identity, which is what you actually want to verify here: not that it's the literal same object, but that its shape and values are correct.

misconceptions.description: toBe and toEqual are interchangeable -- they're just two names for 'check that this value is what I expected.'
misconceptions.clarification: toBe checks strict reference/primitive equality (like ===), while toEqual performs a recursive structural comparison of an object or array's contents. For primitives (numbers, strings, booleans) they behave identically, which is exactly why the distinction goes unnoticed until someone uses toBe on an object or array and gets a confusing failure ('received: {"id":1}, expected: {"id":1}' -- they look identical in the failure output, because the values genuinely are equal in content, just not the same object reference). The rule of thumb: use toBe for primitives, toEqual for objects and arrays.

misconceptions.description: If a test's assertions are wrapped in a describe block, describe itself needs to catch failures, or a failing assertion will crash the whole test file and prevent any other tests from running.
misconceptions.clarification: describe is purely organizational -- it groups related it blocks for readable output, but each individual it/test block is independently isolated by the test runner itself. A failing expect (or a thrown error) inside one it block is caught by Jest, that specific test is marked failed, and Jest proceeds to run every other it block in the file and in every other describe block, completely unaffected. Nothing about describe's presence or absence changes this isolation; it exists at the level of individual test blocks, not describe groupings.

exercises.prompt: Given this test file, which of the three tests pass and which fail when the suite runs? Explain the failure(s).
hints: The first test compares a primitive number with toBe -- is that the right matcher for a primitive?
The second test compares two objects with toBe. Are makeConfig()'s returned object and the literal object passed to toBe ever the SAME object in memory, no matter what properties they share?
toEqual, unlike toBe, compares objects by walking their structure recursively rather than checking if they're the identical reference.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Test 1 passes (retries is a primitive number, and 3 === 3 is true). Test 2 FAILS (toBe on two separately-created objects is always false, regardless of matching contents, because they're different references). Test 3 passes (toEqual compares structure, and both objects have identical keys and values).
exercises.solutionExplanation: makeConfig().retries evaluates to the primitive number 3, and toBe on primitives is equivalent to ===, so 3 === 3 is straightforwardly true -- test 1 passes. Test 2 calls makeConfig() (returning a brand new object) and compares it with toBe against a separate object literal -- even though both objects have identical keys and values, they are two distinct objects in memory, and toBe's reference-equality check (like Object.is) treats any two distinct objects as unequal regardless of their contents, so this test fails. Test 3 uses toEqual instead, which recursively compares the objects' actual structure -- keys and values -- rather than their identity, and since both objects genuinely have retries: 3 and timeout: 1000, this test correctly passes.

exercises.prompt: These two tests pass individually, but fail intermittently depending on which order Jest happens to run them in (or if run in parallel workers). Find the bug and fix it so both tests reliably pass regardless of order.
hints: inventory is declared once, outside both it blocks -- is it being reset anywhere between tests, or is the exact same array being reused and mutated across both tests?
The first test pushes an item onto inventory and never removes it -- if that test runs before the second one, what does the second test's inventory actually contain?
Use beforeEach to reset inventory to a fresh empty array before every single test, rather than relying on the order tests happen to run in.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original inventory array is created exactly once, outside both tests, and the first test mutates it with .push('widget') without ever resetting it -- so if 'adds an item' runs before 'starts empty for a fresh check' (the default file order, but not a guarantee under all Jest configurations), the second test inherits an inventory that already has one item in it, and toHaveLength(0) fails. The fix adds a beforeEach hook that reassigns inventory to a brand-new empty array before every single test runs, completely independent of execution order -- each test now starts from a guaranteed-fresh, empty inventory, so 'adds an item' pushing one item never leaks into any other test's starting state.

assessments.prompt: Why does `expect(getUser()).toBe({ id: 1, name: 'Amy' })` fail even when getUser() genuinely returns an object with exactly those values?
options: toBe only works on primitive values, so using it on any object always throws a TypeError.
toBe checks strict reference equality, and two separately created objects are never the same reference even if their contents are identical -- toEqual is the matcher for structural comparison.
The test is missing an await before getUser(), so it's comparing a Promise to an object.
toBe requires the expected value to be passed as a string, not an object literal.
assessments.explanation: toBe implements strict equality (comparable to ===/Object.is), which for objects and arrays means 'is this the literal same object in memory,' not 'do these two objects have matching contents.' getUser() returns a freshly created object, and the object literal in the test is a second, separate object -- they can never be === to each other no matter how identical their keys and values are. toEqual is the matcher designed for exactly this case: it recursively compares structure instead of checking identity. Option A is wrong -- toBe doesn't throw on objects, it simply (and validly) evaluates to false. Option C is a red herring with no basis in the given code. Option D is false -- toBe accepts any value type, including object literals; it just performs the wrong kind of comparison for this use case.

assessments.prompt: A test suite has ten `it` blocks inside one `describe` block. The third `it` block throws an uncaught error partway through. What happens to the other nine?
options: The whole file stops running immediately -- none of the remaining it blocks execute at all, exactly like an uncaught exception would halt a plain script.

Jest catches the failure within that one it block, marks only that specific test as failed, and continues running every other it block in the file and in any other describe blocks, completely unaffected.
All ten tests inside that same describe block are marked failed as a group, though tests in other, separate describe blocks still run normally.
The remaining tests are skipped entirely and reported as 'pending' rather than actually run or evaluated at all.
assessments.explanation: Each it block is independently isolated by the test runner itself -- a thrown error or failed expect inside one it block is caught by Jest, that one test is marked failed, and Jest proceeds to run every other it block regardless of describe grouping. This is precisely the opposite of a plain script full of sequential code, where an uncaught exception on one line stops everything after it from ever running. Option A describes plain-script behavior, not Jest's. Option C incorrectly assumes failures cascade to sibling tests within the same describe block, which they don't. Option D invents a 'pending' state that doesn't apply here -- the other nine tests run and are evaluated normally.

assessments.prompt: Which of these correctly asserts that calling riskyFunction() throws an error, using Jest's toThrow matcher?
options: expect(riskyFunction()).toThrow('some message');
expect(() => riskyFunction()).toThrow('some message');
expect(riskyFunction).toBe(Error);
expect(riskyFunction()).toEqual(new Error('some message'));
assessments.explanation: toThrow needs to be the one that actually calls the function, inside Jest's own controlled try/catch machinery, so it can observe the throw -- which means you must pass a function reference (here, wrapped in an arrow function) rather than the already-computed result of calling it. Option A calls riskyFunction() immediately, as part of building the expect(...) argument, before Jest's matcher is ever involved -- if it throws there, the throw escapes as an uncaught error in the test itself rather than being cleanly asserted on. Option C compares the function reference itself to the Error constructor, which is nonsensical and unrelated to whether it throws. Option D would suffer the same problem as option A (calling the function immediately) and additionally uses the wrong matcher for asserting a thrown value.

assessments.prompt: A test suite needs (1) an expensive, read-only setup step -- opening one shared database connection used, unmodified, by every test -- and (2) a plain in-memory array reset to empty before every individual test. Which combination of Jest hooks fits each need, respectively?
options: afterAll for the shared connection, afterEach for resetting the array.

beforeAll for the shared, expensive, read-only connection, since it only needs to run once for the whole suite; beforeEach for resetting the mutable array, since it needs a guaranteed-fresh value before every single test.
beforeEach for both, since beforeEach is always the strictly safer choice regardless of what's actually being set up.
describe for the connection, it for the array reset.
assessments.explanation: beforeAll runs once per describe block, which is exactly right for expensive setup that's safe to share, read-only, across every test -- redoing it before every single test would waste time for no benefit. beforeEach runs before every test, which is exactly what a mutated, shared array needs to stay independent between tests -- reusing the same array without resetting it would leak one test's changes into the next. Option A puts the connection's setup in the wrong lifecycle stage (after, not before, and using afterAll's counterpart incorrectly for the array). Option C ignores that beforeEach would redundantly repeat expensive, unnecessary setup work for the read-only connection. Option D confuses hook functions with structural blocks -- describe and it don't function as setup/teardown hooks at all.

assessments.prompt: Explain why tests should be independent of execution order, and how beforeEach helps enforce that -- use a concrete example of what goes wrong when tests silently share mutable state.
assessments.modelAnswer: A test suite's value comes from each individual test reliably reporting pass or fail based solely on the correctness of the code it's actually exercising -- not on which other tests happened to run earlier, in what order, or whether they ran at all (a test runner might filter to run just one test, or shard tests across parallel workers, in either case breaking any assumption about a fixed, complete, sequential run). The moment a piece of mutable state -- a variable, an array, an object -- is declared once and shared across multiple it blocks without being reset, tests stop being independent: one test's side effects (pushing to an array, incrementing a counter, writing to a shared object) become an invisible, undeclared input to whatever test happens to run next. This produces exactly the kind of bug that's maddening to debug, because the test file, read top to bottom, looks completely correct, and running the whole file in its normal order might even pass consistently -- the failure only shows up when tests are reordered, filtered to a subset, or parallelized, which makes it look like the test runner itself is flaky rather than the actual root cause, a hidden dependency between tests. beforeEach solves this directly: by running a fresh setup function immediately before every single it block in its scope, it guarantees each test starts from an identical, known baseline state, regardless of what any previous test did to that same variable. Concretely, reassigning a shared array to a new empty array inside beforeEach (rather than just clearing it with .length = 0 as a side habit, though that also works) means a test that pushes an item and asserts a length of 1 can never accidentally cause a later, unrelated test to see that same leftover item -- each test effectively gets its own private copy of the fixture, even though the variable name is shared across the file.

concepts.title: Mocking Modules and Dependencies
concepts.description: Real code depends on things you don't want a unit test anywhere near -- a live database, a third-party payment API, the current wall-clock time -- and mocking is the technique of swapping those real dependencies for fake, controllable stand-ins so a test can exercise your own logic in isolation, deterministically, without side effects or network calls.
learningObjectives: Explain why a unit test should not make real network calls, hit a real database, or depend on the current time, and what problems each of those causes in a test suite.
Create a mock function with jest.fn(), configure its return value, and assert on how it was called using toHaveBeenCalledWith.
Use jest.mock() to replace an entire module (e.g. a database client or an HTTP client) with a mocked version inside a test file.
Distinguish a mock (a fake with assertions about how it was called) from a stub (a fake that just returns canned data) conceptually, even though libraries blur the line.
Identify when mocking has gone too far -- a test so heavily mocked it no longer verifies real behavior -- and explain the resulting false sense of security.

sections.heading: Why Real Dependencies Don't Belong in a Unit Test
sections.body:
Consider a function that charges a customer's credit card by calling a real payment provider's API, or a function that looks up a user from a real database. Testing either one directly, against the real dependency, has several concrete problems, not just abstract 'purity' concerns. It's **slow** -- a network round trip to a real API is milliseconds to seconds, and a suite with hundreds of tests each making real calls quickly becomes a suite nobody wants to run before every commit. It's **flaky** -- a real service can be down, rate-limited, or slow for reasons that have nothing to do with whether your code is correct, and a test that sometimes fails for reasons unrelated to the code under test trains everyone to ignore failures, which is worse than having no test at all. It's **expensive or dangerous** -- you do not want a test suite that actually charges a real credit card or sends a real email every time CI runs. And it's **hard to control** -- testing 'what happens when the payment API returns a decline' or 'what happens when the database connection times out' against a real service means you'd need to somehow force those exact conditions to occur on demand, which is often impractical or impossible.

Mocking solves all four at once: replace the real dependency with a fake, in-memory stand-in that you fully control, returns instantly, and can be configured to simulate any scenario -- success, failure, a specific edge case -- deterministically, every single run.

sections.heading: jest.fn(): A Mock Function You Can Inspect
jest.mock(): Replacing an Entire Module
Mocks vs Stubs, and When You've Mocked Too Much
sections.body:
The testing literature draws a distinction between a **stub** (a fake that simply returns canned data when called, with no assertions made about how it was called) and a **mock** in the strict sense (a fake you additionally make assertions against -- toHaveBeenCalledWith, toHaveBeenCalledTimes). In practice, especially in the Jest ecosystem, both are commonly just called 'mocks' colloquially, and jest.fn() can be used as either: use it as a stub if you only care about its configured return value, use it as a strict mock if you also assert on the calls made to it. The distinction matters conceptually more than it matters for which Jest API you reach for.

What matters more in practice is not over-mocking. If a test mocks so many pieces of the system under test that what's left being genuinely exercised is a single trivial line of glue code, the test can pass with total confidence while the actual integration between those pieces -- the part most likely to have a real bug -- is never verified at all. A classic version of this: mocking db.getUser to return exactly the shape getUserDisplayName expects, without ever having verified that the real database client actually returns data in that shape. If the real database client's actual response format changes, or never matched that assumption to begin with, every one of these tests keeps passing regardless, and the bug ships to production undetected -- pure false confidence. This is precisely why unit tests with mocked boundaries are usually paired with integration tests (the next concept) that exercise at least one path through the real boundary, catching exactly the class of bug that heavy mocking, by design, cannot.

examples.title: A Mock Function Standing In for a Callback
examples.explanation: processOrder's contract explicitly includes calling onComplete as a side effect, separate from its return value -- a plain expect on the return value alone wouldn't verify that the callback contract is honored at all. jest.fn() gives a fake onComplete with zero real behavior, but Jest records the exact arguments of every call to it, which toHaveBeenCalledWith(35) checks against. toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) additionally guards against a subtly different bug -- one where onComplete gets called correctly, but also gets called an extra, unwanted second time somewhere else in the function, which a check on arguments alone wouldn't catch.

examples.title: Mocking a Module Boundary with jest.mock
examples.explanation: jest.mock('./paymentGateway') intercepts every require of that module inside this test file and replaces its exports with auto-mocked jest.fn() stand-ins -- no real network call to any payment provider happens, ever, no matter how many times this test runs. mockResolvedValue({ status: 'declined' }) configures exactly the scenario that would be awkward or impossible to reliably trigger against a real payment gateway on demand: a genuine decline. expect(...).rejects.toThrow(...) is Jest's matcher for asserting an async function's returned Promise rejects with a matching error, which is exactly what completeCheckout's own logic should do when it sees a non-approved status -- this test verifies completeCheckout's real branching logic, while the payment gateway itself remains entirely faked.

misconceptions.description: Mocking a dependency means you're testing something fake, so a passing test with mocks doesn't really prove anything about your code.
misconceptions.clarification: A mock replaces the dependency, not the code under test -- the actual logic inside the function you're testing (branching, calculations, error handling) still runs for real and is genuinely exercised by the test; only the boundary (a database call, an API request) is faked so you can control exactly what it returns. What a heavily-mocked test does NOT prove is that the real dependency actually behaves the way your mock assumed it would -- that's a real and valid limitation, which is exactly why unit tests with mocked boundaries are complemented by integration tests that exercise at least one path through the real thing, not a reason to dismiss mocking as testing 'nothing real.'

misconceptions.description: jest.mock('./db') only affects the specific require('./db') call written in the same test file -- code inside other files that also require './db' still gets the real module.
misconceptions.clarification: jest.mock('./db') replaces that module for every piece of code loaded within that test file's module resolution, including modules required by the file under test -- if userService.js requires ./db internally, and the test file mocks ./db and then requires userService.js, userService.js's own internal require('./db') resolves to the SAME mocked version, not the real one. This is precisely what makes it possible to test userService's logic while faking its internal database dependency, without userService.js itself needing to know or care that it's running under test.

exercises.prompt: What does this test suite report -- does each test pass or fail, and why?
hints: notifyUser calls sendFn twice in its body -- read the function definition carefully, not just the test names.
toHaveBeenCalledWith only checks that AT LEAST ONE call matched those arguments -- it doesn't care how many total calls were made.
toHaveBeenCalledTimes checks an exact count. If notifyUser calls sendFn twice, what does asserting toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) actually check against?
exercises.expectedAnswer: The first test PASSES (sendFn genuinely was called with (42, 'Hello') -- twice, in fact, but toHaveBeenCalledWith only requires at least one matching call). The second test FAILS, because sendFn was actually called twice, not once -- notifyUser's implementation calls sendFn(userId, message) two separate times.
exercises.solutionExplanation: notifyUser's body calls sendFn(userId, message) twice in a row -- this is a bug in notifyUser itself (presumably it should only notify once), but the test's job is to observe what actually happens, not what should happen. The first test's toHaveBeenCalledWith(42, 'Hello') passes because Jest's matcher checks whether ANY of the recorded calls matched those exact arguments -- both calls did, so this passes regardless of the duplicate. The second test's toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1) checks the exact total call count, which is genuinely 2, not 1, so this assertion fails and correctly surfaces the double-call bug that the first test's matcher was never designed to catch.

exercises.prompt: This test is meant to verify that getUserDisplayName falls back to 'Unknown User' when the mocked database returns null, but it fails with a timeout/assertion error because db.getUser never actually resolves to null as configured. Find and fix the bug.
hints: db.getUser.mockResolvedValue(...) assumes db.getUser is already a jest mock function -- is it? Where is jest.mock('./db') actually called in this file?
Without jest.mock('./db'), require('./db') returns the REAL module, whose getUser is a plain function with no .mockResolvedValue method at all.

jest.mock() calls are typically placed near the top of the test file, before the mocked module is required, so both this test file's own require AND userService.js's internal require resolve to the mocked version.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original test file never calls jest.mock('./db') at all, so require('./db') returns the genuine, real db module -- whose getUser function is an ordinary function, not a jest.fn(), and therefore has no .mockResolvedValue method to call. Calling db.getUser.mockResolvedValue(null) on the real module either throws immediately (mockResolvedValue is not a function) or, depending on the real implementation, silently fails to configure anything, meaning the real db.getUser runs for real and never resolves to null the way the test assumes. Adding jest.mock('./db') before requiring either module tells Jest to auto-mock the db module for this file, turning db.getUser into a genuine jest.fn() with a working .mockResolvedValue -- and because userService.js's own internal require('./db') resolves to that same mocked module, getUserDisplayName's await db.getUser(id) call correctly receives the configured null.

assessments.prompt: A test suite for a checkout function mocks the payment gateway, the email service, and the database so thoroughly that the only code left actually running is a single if statement. All tests pass. What is the most accurate assessment of this test suite?
options: The tests are excellent, since fully isolating the unit under test from every dependency is always the goal of unit testing.

The tests may give false confidence -- if so little of the checkout function's real logic and none of its real dependency behavior is being exercised, the tests mostly confirm the mocks return what they were told to return, not that the system works correctly end to end.
Mocking three dependencies in one test file is invalid -- Jest only supports mocking a single module per test file.
The tests are equivalent to integration tests, since they cover every dependency the function uses.
assessments.explanation: Mocking exists to isolate the code under test from dependencies that are slow, flaky, or hard to control -- but if the mocking is so extensive that almost nothing of the function's OWN logic remains exercised, the tests risk verifying only that the mocks do what they were configured to do, not that the real system behaves correctly when those dependencies are genuinely involved. Option A overstates isolation as an unconditional goal -- isolation is a means to reliable, fast tests, not an end that justifies mocking away the very logic you're trying to verify. Option C is factually wrong -- Jest supports mocking any number of modules in one file. Option D is backwards -- heavy mocking is the opposite of an integration test, which specifically exercises real dependencies rather than replacing them.

assessments.prompt: A function under test awaits a dependency that, in production, performs a real async database call. To simulate that dependency's Promise rejecting with an error in a test, which jest.fn() configuration should be used?
options: mockReturnValue(new Error('...')) -- this hands back the Error object as a resolved value.

mockRejectedValue(new Error('...')) -- this configures the mock to return a Promise that rejects with the given error, which is exactly what an async caller's await needs to actually observe as a failure.
mockImplementation(() => { throw new Error('...'); }) is the only valid way to simulate an async rejection; mockRejectedValue does not exist as a Jest API.
mockReturnValue(Promise.resolve(new Error('...'))) -- wrapping the error in a resolved Promise.
assessments.explanation: mockRejectedValue configures the mock function to return a Promise that specifically rejects with the given value, which is what an awaiting caller needs in order to have its own await throw and its surrounding try/catch (or .catch()) actually engage, faithfully simulating a real async failure. Option A hands back a successfully resolved Promise containing an Error object as data, which is not the same as a rejection -- await would just receive the Error object as a normal value, not throw. Option C is factually wrong -- mockRejectedValue is a real, standard Jest API, specifically for this purpose. Option D similarly produces a resolved Promise, not a rejected one, so an await on it would not throw.

assessments.prompt: A test file calls jest.mock('./db') and then requires userService.js, which itself internally calls require('./db'). Does userService.js's own internal require also resolve to the mocked version, or to the real module?
options: userService.js's internal require always resolves to the real, unmocked module, since jest.mock only affects requires written directly inside the test file itself.

userService.js's internal require resolves to the same mocked version, because jest.mock('./db') replaces that module for every piece of code loaded within the test file's module resolution, including modules required internally by the file under test.
It depends on whether userService.js uses require or import -- only import-based internal dependencies are affected by jest.mock automatically.
userService.js would need to explicitly call jest.mock('./db') itself for its own internal require to be affected; the test file's call alone isn't sufficient.
assessments.explanation: jest.mock('./db') intercepts every require/import of that specific module path within the current test file's entire module graph -- not just the literal line where the test file itself requires it, but every subsequent require of that same path anywhere the test file's requires lead, including inside userService.js. This is exactly what makes it possible to test userService's real logic while faking its internal database dependency, without userService.js needing any awareness that it's running under test. Option A, C, and D all describe a narrower scope than jest.mock actually has, and none matches how module mocking is designed to work.

assessments.prompt: According to the distinction the testing literature draws (even though Jest's own API blurs it in everyday use), what specifically separates a 'stub' from a 'mock' in the strict sense?
options: A stub can only return primitive values, while a mock can return objects and arrays.

A stub is a fake that simply returns canned data when called, with no assertions made about how it was called; a mock (in the strict sense) is a fake you additionally make assertions against -- such as checking it was called with specific arguments, or a specific number of times.
A stub must be created with jest.fn(), while a mock must be created with jest.mock().
A stub always throws an error when invoked, while a mock always returns a successful value.
assessments.explanation: The conceptual distinction is about what you do with the fake afterward: a stub just hands back configured data so the code under test can proceed; a strict mock is additionally the subject of its own assertions -- toHaveBeenCalledWith, toHaveBeenCalledTimes -- verifying the code under test actually interacted with it the expected way. jest.fn() can serve either role depending on whether you assert on its calls. Option A invents a data-type restriction that doesn't exist. Option C is wrong -- both stubs and mocks in this codebase are commonly implemented with jest.fn(); jest.mock() serves an unrelated purpose (replacing an entire module). Option D invents behavior-based categories that have nothing to do with the actual stub/mock distinction.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a developer new to testing why unit tests should mock dependencies like databases and third-party APIs, and also explain the risk of mocking too much -- use a concrete example to illustrate the risk.
assessments.modelAnswer: Real dependencies like a database or a third-party payment API introduce problems that have nothing to do with whether your own code is correct: network calls are slow enough to make a large test suite painfully slow to run, they can fail or behave inconsistently for reasons unrelated to your logic (the service being down, rate limits, network blips), and some operations have real-world side effects you never want happening automatically every time tests run, like actually charging a card or sending an email. Mocking replaces the dependency with a fake, in-memory stand-in that returns instantly and can be configured to simulate any scenario on demand -- including edge cases, like 'the database returns null' or 'the payment gateway declines the charge,' that might be awkward or risky to reliably reproduce against the real thing. The important nuance is that a mock should replace the dependency, not the logic you're actually trying to verify -- a good unit test mocks the boundary (say, db.getUser) while still running the real function under test (say, getUserDisplayName, including its real if/else branching) so that logic genuinely gets exercised. The risk shows up when mocking goes further than that: imagine a checkout test that mocks the payment gateway to always return { status: 'approved' } and mocks the database to always return a valid cart -- if the test suite mocks away every single dependency and every edge case the function might encounter, what's left running might be nothing more than a single line of glue code connecting those mocks together, and the test suite could report 100% passing while never having verified that the real payment gateway's actual response shape matches what the mock assumed, or that the real database's actual error behavior is handled at all. That's false confidence: the tests are green, but they've mostly proven that the mocks do what they were told to do, not that the system works correctly when its real dependencies are actually involved -- which is exactly the gap that integration tests, covered next, are designed to close by exercising at least one real path through those boundaries.

concepts.title: Integration Testing an HTTP API with supertest
concepts.description: A unit test verifies one function in isolation; an integration test verifies that multiple real pieces -- routing, middleware, request parsing, response formatting -- actually work correctly together, and supertest is the standard tool for driving real HTTP requests against an Express app in a test, without needing a separately running server process.
learningObjectives: Explain what an integration test verifies that a unit test with mocked dependencies cannot, using a concrete example.
Write a supertest request against an Express app instance and assert on the response's status code, headers, and body.
Explain why supertest doesn't require calling app.listen() or binding to a real port to test an Express app.
Test both a success path and an error/validation path (e.g. a 400 or 404 response) for a given route.
Structure integration tests so a shared, mutable resource (like a test database or an in-memory store) is reset between tests, mirroring the isolation concerns from unit testing.

sections.heading: What Integration Tests Catch That Unit Tests Don't
sections.body:
The mocking concept ended on a specific limitation: a unit test that mocks a route handler's dependencies proves the handler's own logic is correct given assumptions about what those dependencies return -- it does not prove that Express is actually wired up to call that handler for the right method and path, that a body-parsing middleware is registered before it (so req.body is actually populated), that an auth middleware genuinely blocks an unauthenticated request before it reaches the handler, or that the final JSON sent back over the wire has the status code and shape a real client would actually receive. Every one of those is a question about how multiple pieces of the app are wired together, not about any single function's internal logic -- and that's exactly the gap an **integration test** is designed to close.

Concretely: a route registered as app.get('/users/:id', handler) but accidentally mistyped as app.get('/user/:id', handler) elsewhere would pass every unit test of handler's internal logic with flying colors -- handler itself is perfectly correct -- while being completely unreachable by any real client hitting /users/42. Only a test that actually sends a request through the real Express app and checks the real response would catch a routing mistake like this.

sections.heading: supertest: Driving Real HTTP Requests Without a Real Server
Testing Success and Failure Paths
Isolating State Between Integration Tests
sections.body:
The same independence concerns from unit testing apply here, often with higher stakes, because integration tests frequently touch a real (if test-only) data store rather than a pure in-memory value. If one test creates a user and a later test asserts 'there is exactly one user in the system,' the tests are now coupled through shared, persistent state -- and that coupling breaks the moment tests run in a different order, get filtered, or run in parallel against the same underlying store.

The practical patterns for handling this: use a genuinely separate test database (or an in-memory substitute, like an in-memory SQLite database or a simple in-memory array standing in for a real datastore in a small example app) rather than pointing tests at a real production or shared development database; reset that store's state in a beforeEach so every test starts from a known baseline, exactly as beforeEach reset the plain in-memory cart array in the unit-testing concept; and avoid asserting on absolute counts or IDs that depend on what other tests happened to insert first, preferring assertions scoped to the specific resource a given test itself created or fetched. None of this is unique to integration testing conceptually -- it's the exact same 'don't let tests silently share mutable state' discipline from earlier, just applied to a data layer instead of a plain JavaScript variable, and with a correspondingly bigger cost when it's gotten wrong, since a flaky integration suite is often the first thing a team starts ignoring or disabling under deadline pressure.

examples.title: Testing a Full Express App with supertest
examples.explanation: app.js exports the Express app object itself rather than calling app.listen() -- this separation (app.js defines routes, a separate entry file like server.js calls app.listen()) is exactly what lets the test file import and drive the app directly through supertest without binding any real, fixed port. Both tests exercise the real routing (req.params.id parsing), the real find logic, and the real response formatting end to end -- nothing about users.find or res.json is mocked, because the whole point of this test is to verify those pieces genuinely work together, not to isolate any one of them.

examples.title: Verifying a Body-Parsing Middleware Is Actually Wired Up
examples.explanation: This test would fail with a very specific, useful signal if express.json() were accidentally removed or registered after the /echo route: req.body inside the handler would be undefined, and the echoed response would not match { message: 'hello' } -- exactly the kind of wiring mistake a unit test of an isolated handler function (called directly with a plain object, bypassing the real request-parsing pipeline) would never be able to catch, because it never exercises the actual body-parsing step at all. .send({ message: 'hello' }) with a plain object automatically serializes it to JSON and sets the appropriate Content-Type header, mirroring exactly what a real HTTP client sending a JSON payload would do.

misconceptions.description: You need to call app.listen(someport) before supertest can send requests to your Express app, just like you would to test it manually with curl or a browser.
misconceptions.clarification: supertest is specifically designed NOT to require a running, listening server -- you pass the Express app object itself to request(app), and supertest internally spins up an ephemeral server on a random, unused port for the duration of each request, then tears it down automatically. This is precisely what makes supertest fast and safe to run in parallel test files without any risk of port conflicts; calling app.listen() yourself in a test file is not just unnecessary, it actively works against the pattern most Express apps use for testability, which is exporting the app object separately from whatever entry-point file calls listen() for real deployment.

misconceptions.description: If a route's unit tests (with mocked dependencies) all pass, there's no need for a separate integration test of that same route -- that would just be testing the same logic twice.
misconceptions.clarification: A unit test of a handler's logic and an integration test of the same route verify genuinely different things, not the same thing twice. The unit test proves the handler behaves correctly GIVEN assumptions about how it's invoked and what its mocked dependencies return; it says nothing about whether the route is actually registered at the right path and method, whether the right middleware runs before it in the right order, or whether the real end-to-end request/response cycle produces the status code and body shape a real client needs. A typo in the route's registered path, for instance, would leave every unit test of the handler function passing while making the route completely unreachable in the real app -- only an integration test that sends a real request through the real app would catch that.

exercises.prompt: Given this Express app and test, does the test pass or fail? Explain precisely why, tracing through what the real app actually does with the request.
hints: req.body is only populated by a body-parsing middleware like express.json() -- is that middleware actually registered anywhere in app.js?
Without express.json() registered, what value does req.body have inside the /greet handler when a JSON body is sent?
If req.body is undefined, what does req.body.name evaluate to, and what happens when the handler tries to read a property off of that?
exercises.expectedAnswer: The test FAILS -- not with a mismatched message, but because the request throws an unhandled error inside the handler. Without express.json() registered, req.body is undefined, so req.body.name throws a TypeError ('Cannot read properties of undefined'), and Express responds with a 500 error instead of the expected 200 with a greeting.
exercises.solutionExplanation: app.js never calls app.use(express.json()), so nothing ever parses the incoming request's raw body stream into req.body -- req.body remains undefined for every request, regardless of what the client actually sent. When the /greet handler executes req.body.name, it's attempting to read a property off of undefined, which throws a TypeError synchronously inside the handler. Express's default behavior for a synchronously thrown error in a route handler is to respond with a 500 Internal Server Error, not the 200-with-greeting response the test expects -- so response.status would actually be 500, and expect(response.status).toBe(200) fails. This is exactly the kind of wiring bug (a missing middleware registration) that a unit test calling the handler directly with a plain JS object -- bypassing the real body-parsing step entirely -- would never surface, but that this integration test, which sends a genuine HTTP request through the real app, catches immediately.

exercises.prompt: This integration test suite is meant to test creating users independently, but the second test fails when run after the first one (though it passes fine in isolation). Find the bug and fix it so each test is independent of the others.
hints: The in-memory `users` array lives inside app.js and is shared across every request made to that same app instance for the whole test file -- does anything reset it between tests?
The first test already added Amy to `users` before the second test runs. When the second test adds Ben and then checks the total count, how many users does that array actually contain now?

Rather than asserting an absolute total count (which depends on everything that ran before it), assert something scoped to the specific user this test itself created -- or add a reset mechanism (like a test-only DELETE /users/_reset route, or re-requiring a fresh app module) that runs in beforeEach.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The in-memory `users` array is module-level state living inside app.js, and because both tests require the same already-loaded app module, they share that exact same array across the whole test file -- nothing resets it between tests. The first test adds Amy, leaving one user in the array; the second test then adds Ben, bringing the real total to two, but its assertion assumes the array only ever contains the user it just added, expecting a length of 1 when the actual length is 2. The fix uses jest.resetModules() inside a beforeEach, then re-requires './app' fresh for every test -- since require normally caches a module and returns the same instance on subsequent requires, resetModules is what forces Node to re-evaluate app.js from scratch, giving each test a brand-new, empty `users` array and making the two tests fully independent of run order, exactly mirroring the beforeEach state-reset discipline used for the plain in-memory array in the unit-testing concept.

assessments.prompt: Why does supertest let you write `request(app).get('/health')` without ever calling `app.listen()` in the test file?
options: supertest doesn't actually send real HTTP requests -- it calls the route handler function directly in-process, skipping Express's routing and middleware entirely.

supertest internally starts an ephemeral server on a random available port for the duration of each request and tears it down afterward, so the real Express routing and middleware pipeline runs, without the test needing to manage a fixed port or a long-lived server process.
app.listen() is called automatically the first time the app module is required, before the test file even runs.
supertest requires a real, already-running server on a well-known port, and silently starts one as a background process the first time it's used.
assessments.explanation: supertest takes the Express app object and, per request, spins up a temporary HTTP server bound to an OS-assigned free port, sends a genuine HTTP request to it, captures the real response, and shuts that ephemeral server down -- so the actual routing, middleware, and request/response cycle all run for real, just without the ceremony of a fixed port or manual server lifecycle management. Option A is wrong -- supertest deliberately does exercise the real HTTP/Express pipeline, which is exactly why it can catch wiring bugs like a missing body-parser or a mistyped route path. Option C is wrong -- requiring an Express app module does not call listen() as a side effect; that's precisely why apps are structured to export the bare app object separately from the file that calls listen(). Option D is wrong -- there's no pre-existing well-known-port server involved at all; the port is ephemeral and random per request.

assessments.prompt: A route's handler function is fully correct, and every unit test of it (called directly, with mocked dependencies) passes. But the route was accidentally registered as app.post('/usr', handler) instead of the intended app.post('/user', handler). What does a supertest integration test sending a request to POST /user reveal that the unit tests did not?
options: Nothing different -- since the handler's internal logic is correct, both test types would pass identically.

The integration test receives a 404, because supertest drives a real HTTP request through the real Express app's actual routing table, exposing the mistyped path -- something the unit tests never exercise, since they call the handler function directly and bypass routing entirely.
The integration test also passes, since supertest automatically corrects minor typos in route paths before sending a request.
Express throws a compile-time error before any request is even sent, since it validates every registered route path against a dictionary at startup.
assessments.explanation: A unit test that calls handler directly as a plain function never touches Express's routing table at all -- the typo in app.post('/usr', ...) is completely invisible to it. An integration test sending an actual request to /user through the real app, by contrast, genuinely exercises the routing table, and since no route matches /user (only the mistyped /usr does), Express responds with its default 404, immediately surfacing the bug. Option A ignores that the two test types exercise fundamentally different things. Option C invents autocorrection behavior that doesn't exist. Option D invents a startup-time validation step Express doesn't perform.

assessments.prompt: In a supertest request, what does calling .send({ name: 'Amy' }) on a POST request actually do, and why does that matter for testing whether a body-parsing middleware like express.json() is correctly wired up in the app?
options: It bypasses HTTP entirely and injects the object directly into req.body, so it doesn't actually exercise whether express.json() is registered at all.

It serializes the plain object to JSON and sets the appropriate Content-Type header, sending a genuine JSON request body over the request -- exactly mirroring what a real client would send, so req.body only ends up correctly populated in the handler if express.json() is actually registered and working in the app.
It requires the object to already be manually JSON.stringify'd before being passed in, or supertest throws a TypeError immediately.
It only works for GET requests; POST requests require .attach() instead to include any body data.
assessments.explanation: .send() with a plain object serializes it to JSON and sets Content-Type appropriately, sending a real request body exactly as an actual HTTP client would -- which means the test only sees a correctly populated req.body in the route handler if the app's own body-parsing middleware genuinely runs and works, precisely the kind of wiring a unit test calling the handler directly (with a plain object, bypassing the real parsing step) could never verify. Option A misdescribes .send() as a shortcut that skips the real mechanism, when the whole point is that it doesn't. Option C is wrong -- .send() accepts a plain object and serializes it for you. Option D is wrong -- .send() works with POST (and other body-carrying methods); .attach() is for file uploads specifically, a different use case.

assessments.prompt: Two integration tests in one file both hit a route backed by a shared, module-level in-memory array (let users = [] inside app.js). The first test adds a user; the second test asserts the array's total length is exactly 1, but that assertion fails when the tests run in file order. What is the most robust general fix, consistent with this concept's guidance?
options: Reorder the tests so the length-checking test always runs first, relying on Jest's default file-order execution to keep working indefinitely.

Reset the underlying shared state before every test (for example, via jest.resetModules() and re-requiring the app fresh, or an equivalent reset mechanism), and prefer assertions scoped to the specific resource a test itself created rather than absolute counts that depend on what other tests already did.
Replace toHaveLength(1) with toHaveLength(2) so the assertion matches whatever the actual accumulated count happens to be.
Remove the second test entirely, since asserting on array length is fundamentally incompatible with integration testing.
assessments.explanation: The underlying problem is shared, unreset mutable state leaking between tests -- the same independence concern from unit testing, just applied to a data layer with higher stakes. The robust fix mirrors the unit-testing discipline of resetting state before every test (here, re-requiring a fresh app module so its in-memory array starts empty again) and avoiding assertions that depend on exactly what other tests happened to do first. Option A treats a fragile ordering dependency as a permanent solution, which breaks the moment tests are filtered, reordered, or parallelized. Option C papers over the symptom by hardcoding today's accidental leaked count rather than fixing the actual coupling. Option D throws away a legitimate test rather than fixing the actual state-isolation problem.

assessments.prompt: A teammate says: 'We already have unit tests for every route handler function with all its dependencies mocked -- writing supertest integration tests on top of that is redundant.' Explain what's wrong with this reasoning, with a concrete example of a bug that unit tests would miss but an integration test would catch.
assessments.modelAnswer: Unit tests with mocked dependencies and integration tests verify different layers of correctness, and having thorough coverage of one doesn't make the other redundant. A unit test that calls a route handler function directly, with mocked dependencies, proves that GIVEN a request object shaped a certain way and GIVEN that its dependencies return certain values, the handler's own internal logic produces the right output -- but it necessarily assumes away everything about how that handler actually gets invoked in the real app: whether it's registered at the correct URL and HTTP method, whether the middleware that's supposed to run before it (body parsers, auth checks) is actually registered and in the right order, and whether the real request/response cycle -- real headers, real status codes, real serialized JSON -- comes out the way a real client needs. A concrete example: suppose a route is meant to be registered as app.post('/users', createUserHandler), but someone accidentally writes app.post('/user', createUserHandler) -- a one-character typo, missing the plural 's'. Every unit test of createUserHandler itself would continue to pass without any change at all, because those tests call createUserHandler directly, as a plain function, and never go anywhere near Express's actual routing table where the typo lives. But a real client, or a real integration test, sending a POST request to the correct path /users would get a 404, because that route was never actually registered under that path in the first place. Only an integration test that drives an actual HTTP request through the real Express app -- exactly what supertest is for -- exercises the routing table itself and would catch this immediately, which is precisely why integration tests complement rather than duplicate unit tests: they cover the wiring and composition of pieces that isolated, mocked unit tests are specifically designed to skip over.
